12. TERM / TENURE

The term / tenure of the Directors shall be governed as per provisions of the applicable laws, as amended from time to time and as follows: -

1. Managing Director / Whole-time Director / Manager (Managerial Person): -

The Company shall appoint or re-appoint any person as its Managerial Person for a term up to five years at a time. No re-appointment shall be made earlier than one year before the expiry of term.

2. Independent Director: -

An Independent Director may hold office for a term up to five consecutive years on the Board of the Company and will be eligible for re-appointment on passing of a special resolution by the Company and disclosure of such appointment in the Board's report.

No Independent Director shall hold office for more than two consecutive terms, however, such Independent Director shall be eligible for appointment after expiry of three years of ceasing to become an Independent Director. Provided that an Independent Director shall not, during the said period of three years, be appointed in or be associated with the Company in any other capacity, either directly or indirectly.

13. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION

The Committee shall specify the manner for effective evaluation of performance of the Board, its Committees and individual directors of the Company with the aim to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of the Board and Committees.

The Board of Directors shall carry out the performance evaluation of every individual director except the director being evaluated, along with its various Board Committees and Board as whole. Further, performance evaluation shall be carried out at least once in a year in accordance with the manner prescribed in Annexure 2 hereto.

The performance evaluation of KMPs (excluding executive directors) shall be performed by Nomination & Remuneration Committee and of SMPs by the Compensation Committee of the Company, on annual basis or at the time of salary appraisals and in compliance with the Articles of Association of the Company.

14. POLICY ON DIVERSITY OF THE BOARD

a. The Company acknowledges the importance of diversity at the Board. Diversity encompasses diversity of perspective, experience, education, background, ethnicity and personal attributes. The Company recognizes that gender diversity is a significant aspect of diversity and acknowledges the role that woman with skills and experience can play in contributing to diversity of perspective at the Board. Other relevant matters such as independence and the ability to fulfil required time commitments in the case of Independent and Non-Executive Directors will also be taken into account;

<!-- image -->

b. The Committee shall review and evaluate Board composition to ensure that the Board have the appropriate mix of skills, experience, independence and knowledge to ensure their continued effectiveness. The Committee will ensure that no person is discriminated against on grounds of religion, race, gender, national origin or ancestry, marital status, age, or any other personal or physical attribute as a Board member; and
c. To ensure Board diversity at broad level, the Company shall provide sufficient information to the shareholders about the qualifications, expertise and characteristics of each Board Member.

15. REMOVAL / RETIREMENT

Owning to reasons for any disqualification mentioned in the applicable law, the Committee may recommend to the Board with reasons recorded in writing, removal of a Director and KMP subject to the provisions and compliance of the Applicable Law.

The Director and KMP shall retire as per the provisions of the applicable law and in accordance with the Human Resource Policy of the Company. The Board will have the discretion to retain the Director and KMP in the same position/remuneration or otherwise even after attaining the retirement age, for the benefit of the Company subject to such approvals as may be required in this regard.

Further, the Removal/ Retirement/ Retrenchment of SMPs shall be decided by either of Managing Director or Executive Director or CEO / CFO (whomsoever is the reporting authority) in accordance with the Human Resource Policy of the Company.

16. SUCCESSION PLANNING

'Succession Planning' means making the necessary arrangements to ensure that suitably qualified people are available to fill posts which will arise within any specific department over forthcoming years. The succession planning is implemented by the management, the Committee of the Company, the Board, the Human Resources Department, and the employees themselves.

17. VALIDITY

The Policy shall be valid till next review by Committee members and/or Board of Directors, as applicable.

18. REVIEW

The Company's CEO, CFO and COO have been entrusted with the responsibility of enforcement of this Policy. They are hereby given absolute power to jointly or severely, make necessary changes, amendments or additions or removals for the operational aspects of the policy within the overall spirit and guidance from time to time for reasons like technology or process upgradation, regulatory changes, maintaining competitive edge or responding to changes in market or risk environment, etc. This is required to ensure full operational freedom to the senior management and make the management team more adaptive to rapid changing external environment. All changes so made shall be noted to the policy approving authority during the next policy review.

The CEO, CFO and COO can decide on delegation of authority and can design / redesign MIS systems and reporting as they see fit to improve the responsibility and accountability within the team hierarchy.

ANNEXURE 1 - FIT & PROPER POLICY

1. ABOUT THE POLICY

Pursuant to RBI Guidelines, the Board of Directors ('Board') of KFL, has adopted the Fit and Proper Policy ('Policy') regarding ascertaining the Fit and Proper criteria of Directors at the time of their appointment and on continuing basis. This Policy is to ensure that the Directors of the Company who are responsible for steering the affairs of the Company are fit and proper, besides having the necessary qualifications.

2. GUIDELINES ON 'FIT & PROPER'

The Nomination & Remuneration Committee ('Committee') shall ensure that prior to considering any candidature for appointment, re-appointment as a Director on the Board of the Company, detailed due diligence is undertaken to consider suitability of the Candidate. Such due diligence shall be based on:

i. Qualification of the candidate
ii. Technical Expertise and competence of the candidate
iii. Track record of the candidate
iv. Integrity of the candidate
v. Reputation and character of the candidate
vi. Any other parameters that the Committee may deem fit to analyse

Further statutory declarations/Appendix XXIII-A as prescribed in the Master Directions shall be obtained from Directors before appointment/re-appointment and on annual basis. The Committee shall scrutinize the declarations and the chairperson of the Committee may thereafter add remarks on the declaration.

3. EVALUATION OF 'FIT & PROPER'

3.1 Before appointing any person as a director on the Board or continuing the appointment of any such director, the Committee shall undertake adequate due diligence in respect of such individuals to ascertain suitability on the basis of the qualification, expertise, track record, integrity of such individual and also such other factors in respect of which information is obtained by the Company in the Declaration and Undertaking.
3.2 The Company shall, prior to the appointment of any person as a director on the Board and/or from the existing directors, obtain necessary information and declarations in the format as given in the Master Directions or such other format (where applicable) which may be prescribed for this purpose by the RBI, from time to time ('Declaration and Undertaking'). These Declaration and Undertaking shall be obtained from all the directors within the prescribed timelines.
3.3 The Committee shall scrutinize each Declarations and Undertakings and thereafter, considering the result of its due diligence and the information provided in the signed Declarations and Undertakings, decide and recommend the same to the Board the acceptance or otherwise about the potential new directors or existing directors, whose appointment is to be continued or renewed, as the case may be.
3.4 Without limiting the generality of the foregoing paragraphs:

In accordance with the provisions of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Rules, 2017, Kogta Financial (India) Limited ('Company') is committed to providing equal opportunity in employment and creating an inclusive working environment for all individuals, including persons with disabilities.

Our policy states there should be no discrimination, harassment, or less favorable treatment for the persons with disabilities.

2 Scope and Applicability

The Company's Equal Opportunity Policy covers all individuals with disabilities, including job applicants, fulltime and part-time employees, interns and trainees, contractual employees, and temporary staff. This policy also includes employees who acquire a disability during their tenure with the Company. The policy applies to all aspects of employment, including but not limited to recruitment, training, working conditions, salaries and allowances, facilities and perquisites, transfers, employee welfare, career development, disciplinary matters, and terminal benefits.

Welcome to the Find the Path project. The goal of the project is to implement a solver for the mini-game explained in the requirements below. 

Your task is to find the shortest path in the code matrix that contains sequences with the largest total score. A path is basically a list of matrix cells that are connected to each other. Length of a path means the number of cells in the list. The shorter the path – the fewer cells it has. The picture below demonstrates the solved puzzle with the resulting path marked in red.

Here, we have a path 3A-10-9B, which is 3 cells in length. This path contains the given sequence 3A-10-9B that earns you 10 score points. In this simplest example the path actually matches the sequence. More complex puzzles typically have longer paths containing various different sequences at once.
 
The rules for solving the puzzle are explained in the next section.
 
Solving the Puzzle
Let’s look at the example above. Here, we have only one sequence 3A-10-9B. The goal is to pick the proper cells from the code matrix in proper order to piece together the given code sequence. 
 
The trick is that you can’t choose completely arbitrary cells. You must always start with the top row. Here, we have 5 possible codes to choose from: 3A, 3A, 10, 9B and 72. Suppose you have selected 3A in the second column. It perfectly matches the first element of our code sequence.

Next, you need to choose one cell from the same column as the previous cell you picked. In our case, this is the second column. Let’s pick code 10 in the fourth row matching the second element in our sequence. Finally, you need to pick code 9B from the fourth row to complete the sequence.

And that’s it. Congratulations on the first solved puzzle! Let’s summarize the learned rules:
 
 At any given moment, you can only choose cells in a specific column or row.
On each turn, you need to switch between column and row, and you have to stay on the same line as the previous cell you picked. This is similar to Snake game. You have to move at right angles.
You always start with picking the first cell from the top row, then you always go vertically down in order to pick the second cell, and then you continue switching between column and row as usual.
You can’t choose the same cell twice. The resulting path must not contain duplicated cells.
The number of picked cells must not exceed the maximum allowed length of the path.
 
Multiple Sequences
There can be more than one sequence to complete. The picture below demonstrates the solution for a puzzle with two sequences. You can complete sequences in any order. The order in which the sequences are listed doesn’t matter.
 
Wasted Moves
Sometimes we are forced to waste moves and choose additional cells that don’t belong to any sequence. Let’s look at the following example.
The sequences 10-D4-72-72 and 3A-10-D4 start with codes 10 and 3A respectively, but there are no such cells in the first row at all! To deal with this issue, we have to waste one move and choose any other cell, e.g., 72 in the third column. After that we will be able to continue moving and successfully complete both sequences. The length of the resulting path, including wasted moves, is 6 cells which still fit the given limit.
 
Notice how the two sequences “overlap” in the resulting path. This is perfectly fine. The more overlapping between sequences – the shorter the resulting path.
 
In some cases, one wasted move is not enough and we need to waste more of them. The next picture shows a tricky case with three wasted moves in total!

Here, we have to waste one move before the sequence 3A-9B and two moves between sequences 3A-9B and 72-D4. Also notice how red lines between 3A and 9B as well as between 72 and D4 “cross” previously selected cells D4 and 9B respectively. This is perfectly allowed. You can pick different cells from the same row or column multiple times.
 
Let’s summarize the rules shown above:
 
You can waste 1 or 2 moves before the first sequence.
You can also waste 1 or 2 moves between any neighboring sequences.
However, you cannot break sequences and waste moves in the middle of them.
 
Competing Sequences
Sometimes it isn’t possible to complete all sequences at once within the given path length limit. In this case you have to choose which sequences to complete and which sequences to ignore. This is the time when sequence scores come into play. If you have to choose between multiple sequences, always prefer sequences with the largest sum of scores.
 
For instance, on the following picture we can complete either 9B-3A-72-D4 or 72-D4-3A but not both of them due to the maximum path length of 5 cells. We have chosen the sequence 9B-3A-72-D4 since it grants more score points than 72-D4-3A.

Puzzles Without a Solution
Finally, there might be puzzles that have no solution at all.
 
Example of a puzzle without any solution 
 
The first sequence 3A-D4 can’t be completed since code matrix doesn’t contain code D4 at all. The second sequence 72-10 can’t be completed for another reason: codes 72 and 10 aren’t located in the same row or column anywhere in the matrix, and therefore can’t form a sequence.
 
Technical Details / Requirements
To get started please read the README file at the root of the Git repository. Additional details about building and running the project can be found there.
 
Existing Source Code
Even though this is a new project you will not be starting from scratch. In the repository you will also find some preexisting source code. You must continue building on top of that preexisting source code and you should NOT DELETE any of the existing source code, files and folders NOR move or rename any of the existing files, classes, methods or variables. However, you’re free to add new source files to the project and extend existing classes with your own methods and variables. 
 
The project provides several existing classes that you should use in your work:
 
Matrix represents a code matrix with arbitrary dimensions.
Sequence stores a required sequence of codes along with their scores.
Path represents a path in the code matrix. It consists of multiple Position objects.
Position refers to a particular row and column in the code matrix.
PathFinder is a puzzle solver class. It has a method named run() that you need to implement.
 
Solver Implementation
The PathFinder.run() method requires you to calculate the shortest path in the code matrix that contains sequences with the largest total score.
 
The dimensions of the code matrix, number of sequences and length of sequences can be arbitrary. Your code shouldn’t impose any artificial limits on them.
 
While developing the algorithm, use the following rules to compare different paths and determine the resulting one:
 
When comparing different paths, always choose one that yields more score than another. For instance, a path with one completed sequence that earns 50 points is better than a path with two completed sequences that earns 30 points in total.
If you have multiple paths with the same score, choose the shortest one, i.e., having fewer cells than another. The geometric distance between neighboring cells doesn’t matter.
Finally, if you have multiple paths with the same score and length, return any one of them.
 
Performance Considerations
There are multiple ways to implement the puzzle solving algorithm. 
 
One of them is to generate all possible paths in the code matrix, loop through them and choose the best one. This is the easiest but also the slowest approach. Solving larger matrices with larger maximum length of path might take dozens of minutes, if not hours. If you correctly implement such an algorithm, the automatic grading system will accept your solution with an average score which would be enough to successfully pass the challenge. 
 
If the simplest approach feels too easy to you and you want to achieve a perfect grade, try to implement a faster algorithm that doesn’t iterate through all possible paths and can solve puzzles with the following parameters in less than 10 seconds:
 
Matrix size: 10x10
Number of sequences: 5
Average length of sequences: 4
Maximum path length: 12
At least one solution exists 
 
Error Handling
Your code should properly validate input parameters, handle errors and throw exceptions. The project provides the following exception classes:
 
InvalidArgumentError. Throw it if some of input parameters are incorrect. You should validate the following conditions:
Code matrix should be non-empty
There should be at least one sequence
All sequences should be non-empty
All sequences should have a score greater than zero
Maximum path length should be greater than zero
PathNotFoundError. Throw it if you can’t find any suitable path in the code matrix, i.e., the puzzle doesn’t have a solution.
 
Testing Your Work
In order to help you test your work, the project provides a small command-line utility with a single Application class. It basically runs PathFinder on different puzzles and prints their solutions or errors to the console.
 
Unlike other preexisting classes, you can freely modify the source code of Application class and write your own test cases. Please use it to carefully test your algorithm on various matrices and sequences before submitting the final code.
 
Good luck!

 Algorithm 

 We'll use a Depth-First Search (DFS) approach to explore possible paths. 

 Initialization: 

 Start at each cell in the top row of the matrix. 

 Keep track of the current path, the completed sequences, and the total score. 

 Use a visited set to avoid revisiting cells. 

 Recursive DFS Function: 

 Base Case: 

 If all sequences are completed, or the maximum path length is reached, evaluate the path. 

 Recursive Step: 

 For the current cell, find valid neighbors (same row or column, not visited). 

 For each neighbor:

 Add it to the current path. 

 Update completed sequences and score. 

 Recursively call DFS on the neighbor. 

 Remove the neighbor from the path (backtracking). 

 Path Evaluation: 

 Calculate the total score of completed sequences. 

 If it's higher than the best score, update the best path. 

 If scores are equal, choose the shorter path. 

 Python Code 

 class PathFinder:
 def __init__(self, matrix, sequences, max_path_length):
 self.matrix = matrix
 self.sequences = sequences
 self.max_path_length = max_path_length
 self.rows = len(matrix)
 self.cols = len(matrix[0])
 self.best_path = None
 self.best_score = -1

 def run(self):
 for col in range(self.cols):
 self._dfs([(0, col)], set([(0, col)]), 0, [])
 if not self.best_path:
 raise Exception("Path not found")
 return self.best_path

 def _dfs(self, path, visited, score, completed_sequences):
 if len(path) > self.max_path_length:
 return

 current_code = self.matrix[path[-1][0]][path[-1][1]]
 new_completed_sequences = self._update_completed_sequences(completed_sequences, current_code)
 new_score = self._calculate_score(new_completed_sequences)

 if new_score > self.best_score or (new_score == self.best_score and len(path) < len(self.best_path or [])):
 self.best_score = new_score
 self.best_path = path[:]

 if len(new_completed_sequences) == len(self.sequences) or len(path) == self.max_path_length:
 return

 row, col = path[-1]
 if len(path) % 2 == 1: # Move in the same column
 for r in range(self.rows):
 if (r, col) not in visited:
 self._dfs(path + [(r, col)], visited | {(r, col)}, new_score, new_completed_sequences)
 else: # Move in the same row
 for c in range(self.cols):
 if (row, c) not in visited:
 self._dfs(path + [(row, c)], visited | {(row, c)}, new_score, new_completed_sequences)

 def _update_completed_sequences(self, completed_sequences, current_code):
 new_completed_sequences = completed_sequences[:]
 for i, seq in enumerate(self.sequences):
 if i not in new_completed_sequences:
 if len(seq) > 0 and seq[0] == current_code:
 if len(seq) == 1:
 new_completed_sequences.append(i)
 else:
 self.sequences[i] = seq[1:]
 return new_completed_sequences

 def _calculate_score(self, completed_sequences):
 score = 0
 for i in completed_sequences:
 score += self.sequences[i][-1] # Assuming score is the last element
 return score

 Explanation 

 PathFinder Class: 

 Stores the matrix, sequences, and maximum path length. 

 run() initializes the DFS and returns the best path. 

 _dfs() Function: 

 Performs the depth-first search. 

 path is the current list of cell coordinates. 

 visited is a set of visited cell coordinates. 

 score is the current total score. 

 completed_sequences is a list of completed sequence indices. 

 Updates completed sequences and scores. 

 Recursively calls itself on valid neighbors. 

 _update_completed_sequences() Function: 

 Checks if the current code matches the start of any sequence. 

 If it does, updates the sequence and adds it to completed_sequences if finished. 

 _calculate_score() Function: 

 Calculates the total score of the completed sequences. 

 How to Use 

 Create a PathFinder object with the matrix, sequences, and maximum path length. 

 Call run() to get the best path.

 ["9B", "72", "3A", "10", "72"],
 ["10", "3A", "3A", "3A", "10"],
 ["3A", "10", "3A", "9B", "72"],
 ["10", "10", "3A", "72", "72"]
]
sequences = [["3A", "10", "9B", 10]] # Sequence with score
max_path_length = 3

finder = PathFinder(matrix, sequences, max_path_length)
path = finder.run()
print(path) # Output: [(0, 0), (3, 0), (3, 3)]

 Key Improvements 

 DFS: Explores all possible paths. 

 Backtracking: Avoids redundant exploration. 

 Score and Length Optimization: Finds the best path based on score and length.

Standard Operating Procedure: TF-Serving Model Deployment 

 This document outlines the end-to-end process for deploying, updating, and managing TensorFlow Serving (TF-Serving) models in production environments. 

 1. Prerequisites and Environment Setup 

 Before handling models or validating layers, ensure your local or test environment is properly configured. 

 Python Environment 

 Create a virtual environment using Python 3.8. 

 Install the required dependencies:
 pip install absl-py==0.15.0 astunparse==1.6.3 cached-property==1.5.2 cachetools==4.2.4 certifi==2023.11.17 charset-normalizer==2.0.12 clang==5.0 dataclasses==0.6 flatbuffers==1.12 gast==0.3.3 google-auth==1.35.0 google-auth-oauthlib==0.4.6 google-pasta==0.2.0 grpcio==1.32.0 h5py==2.10.0 idna==3.6 importlib-metadata==4.8.3 keras==2.6.0 Keras-Preprocessing==1.1.2 Markdown==3.3.7 numpy==1.19.5 oauthlib==3.2.2 opt-einsum==3.3.0 protobuf==3.19.6 pyasn1==0.5.1 pyasn1-modules==0.3.0 requests==2.27.1 requests-oauthlib==1.3.1 rsa==4.9 six==1.15.0 tensorboard==2.6.0 tensorboard-data-server==0.6.1 tensorboard-plugin-wit==1.8.1 tensorflow==2.4.0 tensorflow-estimator==2.4.0 termcolor==1.1.0 typing-extensions==3.7.4.3 urllib3==1.26.18 Werkzeug==2.0.3 wrapt==1.12.1 zipp==3.6.0

 Model Verification 
To verify the input and output layers of the provided model (required for flask_pp updates), navigate to the model directory and run: 

 saved_model_cli show --dir . --all

 2. Infrastructure Connection Protocol 

 Step 2.1: Connect to the Bastion VM 
Use the appropriate gcloud compute ssh command for your target environment (see Appendix A for the full list of connection strings).
 Example for DKYC Prod: 

 gcloud compute ssh jiovishwam-production-bastion-vm-1 --project jiovishwamprod --zone asia-south1-a

 Step 2.2: Connect to the NFS VM 
Once inside the Bastion, connect to the internal NFS VM where the models reside. 

 gcloud compute ssh jiovishwam-production-nfs-vm-1 --internal-ip --zone asia-south1-a

 Navigate to the models directory: cd /tf_models (or the specific path for the target deployment). 

 Step 2.3: Connect to the Kubernetes Cluster 
In a separate terminal (or after configuring the VM), authenticate with the target Kubernetes cluster to manage deployments.
 Example for DKYC Prod Cluster: 

 gcloud container clusters get-credentials jiovishwam-production-cluster-1 --region asia-south1 --project jiovishwamprod

 3. Model Retrieval & File Transfer 

 The ML team pushes zipped model files to a centralized cloud storage bucket. 

 Locate the required model files in the storage bucket. A valid TF model folder must contain:

 saved_model.pb file 

 variables/ folder 

 Copy the model from the bucket to the NFS VM using gsutil (for GCP) or azcopy (for Azure).
 # GCP Copy Command
sudo gsutil cp -r gs://<source-bucket-path> <destination-vm-path>

 4. Directory Structure & Configuration (The Core Process) 

 Depending on whether this is a new model entirely or a version update to an existing model, the workflow splits into two scenarios. 

 Scenario A: Version Update (Existing Model) 

 If updating an already deployed model for an existing customer: 

 Navigate to the existing model folder. 

 Identify the latest version number (e.g., if folders 1 , 2 , 3 exist, your new version will be 4 ). 

 Create the new version directory.
 mkdir 4

 Move the .pb file and variables folder inside this new version directory. 

 No Restart Required: TF-Serving automatically polls for new version directories. The new model will be picked up within 1-2 minutes without needing a pod restart. 

 Scenario B: Deploying a New Model (New Customer / New Pipeline) 

 If adding a completely new model that is not currently tracked by TF-Serving: 

 Create a new root directory for the model. 

 Create a 1 folder inside it for the initial version, and place the .pb and variables inside. 

 Backup the Configuration: Before making any edits, always snapshot the existing config.conf file.
 cp config.conf config_backup_<MM_DD_YYYY>.conf

 Edit config.conf : Open config.conf and append the new model's JSON block (name, base path, model platform). 

 Restart Required: Because the configuration file has been modified, the TF-Serving Kubernetes deployment must be restarted to read the new config.conf . 

 5. Deployment Restart & Verification 

 Restarting the Deployment (Only for Scenario B) 
Use kubectl to rollout or restart the specific TF-serving deployment. 

 Log Verification 
Check the logs of the newly spawned pod to ensure successful initialization. 

 kubectl get pods -n <namespace>
kubectl logs <pod-name> -n <namespace>

 Success Indicator: Look for the phrase "entering the event loop" in the logs. This confirms TF-Serving has successfully loaded the models and is ready to accept gRPC/REST requests. 

 Troubleshooting Volume Mounts 
If the naming convention of the deployments is ambiguous and you need to verify which Persistent Volume (PV) or folder is attached to a specific deployment: 

 Check the deployments to find the associated PVC. 

 Describe the Persistent Volume to see the exact NFS path it mounts.
 kubectl describe pv <PV-ID>

 Just as we made the server-side tool creation dynamic, we can do the same for this client-side test script. By moving the test definitions into a separate YAML file, your Python script becomes a simple, generic test runner that never needs to be modified when you add new tests. 

 Here is the refactored, configuration-driven approach. 

 Step 1: Create the Test Cases Configuration File 

 First, create a single YAML file to define all your test cases. Each test case will specify the tool's name, its ID, the payload to send, and a description. This completely separates your test data from your test logic .

 Step 2: Refactor the example.py Script 

 Now, replace your existing example.py with this much shorter and smarter version. This script loads all tests from test_cases.yaml and runs them dynamically. 

 refactored_example.py : 

 import os
import json
import sys
import argparse
import asyncio
import yaml

from mcp import ClientSession
from mcp.client.sse import sse_client
from helpers.helper import extract_and_pretty, read_image_as_b64

def load_test_cases(filepath="test_cases.yaml"):
 with open(filepath, "r") as f:
 return yaml.safe_load(f)

async def run_test_case(session, test_case, enabled_tools):
 tool_name = test_case["name"]
 description = test_case["description"]

 if enabled_tools and tool_name not in enabled_tools:
 print(f"{description}: SKIPPED (disabled in .env)")
 return

 payload = test_case["payload"]

 # Handle local image loading before calling the tool
 if "image_src" in payload and os.path.exists(payload["image_src"]):
 payload["image_src"] = read_image_as_b64(payload["image_src"])

 res = await session.call_tool(tool_name, payload)
 print(f"{description}:", extract_and_pretty(res))

async def main(chosen_tool=None, server="http://localhost:8001/mcp"):
 try:
 enabled_tools = {t.lower() for t in json.loads(os.getenv("ENABLED_TOOLS", "[]"))}
 except (json.JSONDecodeError, TypeError):
 enabled_tools = set()

 test_cases = load_test_cases()
 test_map = {str(tc["id"]): tc for tc in test_cases}
 test_map.update({tc["name"].lower(): tc for tc in test_cases})

 async with sse_client(url=f"{server}/sse") as (r, w):
 async with ClientSession(r, w) as session:
 await session.initialize()

 if chosen_tool and chosen_tool != "list":
 test_to_run = test_map.get(chosen_tool.lower())
 if test_to_run:
 await run_test_case(session, test_to_run, enabled_tools)
 else:
 print(f"Unknown tool: {chosen_tool}")
 else:
 print("\n=== Tool Test Case Status ===")
 for tc in test_cases:
 status = "ENABLED" if not enabled_tools or tc["name"] in enabled_tools else "disabled"
 print(f" Tool #{tc['id']:<2}: {tc['name']:<35} -> {status}")
 print("=============================\n")
 if chosen_tool is None:
 for tc in test_cases:
 await run_test_case(session, tc, enabled_tools)

if __name__ == "__main__":
 parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Run MCP tool tests from a config file.")
 parser.add_argument("-t", "--tool", nargs="?", const="list", help="Tool ID or name to run.")
 parser.add_argument("-s", "--server", default="http://localhost:8001/mcp")
 args = parser.parse_args()

 try:
 asyncio.run(main(chosen_tool=args.tool, server=args.server))
 except KeyboardInterrupt:
 sys.exit(0)
 except FileNotFoundError:
 print("Error: test_cases.yaml not found. Please create it.")

 Advantages of this New Approach 

 Zero Code Changes : To add a new test (like for our dynamic get_user_info tool), you only add a new entry to test_cases.yaml . You never have to touch the Python script again. 

 Clean and Readable : The Python script is now a generic engine. All the messy, specific test data is neatly organized in the YAML file. 

 Easier to Manage : It's much simpler to view, edit, or disable tests by just editing the YAML configuration. 

 Less Error-Prone : You avoid the risk of introducing syntax errors into the Python script's logic when adding new tests.

Readme.md:
# FR Jio Models Test Harness

This repository is used to:

1. Convert Face Recognition production models from **FR 36 format** to **TensorFlow 2.16 compatible formats**.
2. Export converted models for **TensorFlow Serving** usage.
3. Validate that FR 36 and TF 2.16 predictions are aligned.
4. Store verification CSVs for model-by-model comparison.

---

## 1) Folder Structure (Detailed)

Below is the project structure and what each part is used for.

### Root: `Fr_jio_models_test_harness`

- `Readme.md` 
 Project documentation.

- `conversion_json_architecture/` *(helping_folder)* 
 Shared JSON model architecture template:
 - `siamese_face_model_tf_216.json`

- `2_16_model_validation_scripts/` 
 Validation scripts for scoring and comparison:
 - `trained/` *(helping_folder for temporary/aux files)*
 - `fr_36_score_validator.py`
 - `tf_2_16_score_validator.py`
 - `tf_serving_tf_2_16_validator.py`

- `convert_model_from_json_to_tfserving.py` 
 Converts/builds model export for TF Serving format.

- `convert_old_models_to_tf_216.py` 
 Converts old FR 36 `.h5` models into TF 2.16 compatible artifacts.

- `sample_500_data/` *(testing_dataset)* 
 Test dataset used for validation and score comparison.

- `jio_prod_models/` 
 Main model store by business stream (`dkyc`, `ekyc`, `mhere`, `skyc`).
 Each stream has:
 - `production (fr_36)/` → original FR 36 `.h5` models
 - `tf_216/` → converted model outputs:
 - `complete_h5_models/`
 - `complete_keras_models/`
 - `json_architecture_and_weights/`
 - `tf_216_architecture_file/siamese_face_model_tf_216.json`
 - `*.weights.h5`
 - `tfserving/` (serving-export-ready model folders/files)

- `verification_csv/` 
 Final comparison outputs (per stream + per model):
 - FR 36 prediction CSVs
 - TF Serving prediction CSVs
 - Combined comparison CSVs (`complete_fr36_and_tf216_scores.csv` pattern)

- `fr_36_requirements.txt` 
 Dependencies for FR 36 environment.

- `tf_216_requirements.txt` 
 Dependencies for TF 2.16 environment.

---

## 2) Model Storage Pattern (How to read each stream folder)

For each stream (`dkyc`, `ekyc`, `mhere`, `skyc`):

1. **`production (fr_36)`** 
 Source/original trained models (`.h5`) from old pipeline.

2. **`tf_216/complete_h5_models`** 
 Full model saved again as complete `.h5` in TF 2.16 compatible style.

3. **`tf_216/complete_keras_models`** 
 Full model saved in `.keras` format.

4. **`tf_216/json_architecture_and_weights`** 
 Architecture + weights separated:
 - shared architecture JSON
 - per-model `*.weights.h5`

5. **`tf_216/tfserving`** 
 Model artifacts prepared for serving deployment/testing.

---

## 3) Conversion Files (Detailed)

## `convert_old_models_to_tf_216.py`

### Purpose
Converts legacy FR 36 model files into TensorFlow 2.16 compatible outputs.

### Typical role in pipeline
- Read old production `.h5` model(s).
- Rebuild/load architecture for TF 2.16 (using JSON where needed).
- Save outputs into multiple formats:
 - complete `.h5`
 - complete `.keras`
 - split architecture + weights (`*.weights.h5`)

## `convert_model_from_json_to_tfserving.py`

### Purpose
Takes TF 2.16-compatible model (typically architecture + weights or rebuilt model) and exports it for TensorFlow Serving workflow.

### Typical role in pipeline
- Load TF 2.16 model representation.
- Build final serving artifact.
- Write output into:
 - `jio_prod_models/<stream>/tf_216/tfserving/`

### Why this exists separately
- One script focuses on conversion to TF 2.16 formats.
- This script focuses on deployment-ready/serving-ready export.

---

## 4) `2_16_model_validation_scripts` Working (Simple Explanation)

Validation scripts check whether converted model behavior matches the original FR 36 behavior.

## `fr_36_score_validator.py`
- Runs inference using original FR 36 model(s).
- Uses Fr_36 Environment and dependencies.
- Uses `sample_500_data` as input.
- Produces FR 36 baseline prediction CSV.

## `tf_2_16_score_validator.py`
- Runs inference using converted TF 2.16 model(s).
- Uses TF 2.16 Environment and dependencies.
- Uses same `sample_500_data` for input.
- Compares/aligns results with FR 36 baseline.
- Produces combined score comparison CSV (FR 36 vs TF 2.16).

## `tf_serving_tf_2_16_validator.py`
- Validates predictions from TF Serving-exported model.
- Uses TF 2.16 Environment and dependencies.
- Uses same `sample_500_data` for input.
- Used to confirm serving output is consistent with local TF 2.16 and FR 36 expectations.
- Produces TF Serving prediction CSV and/or merged comparison CSV (per setup in script).

---

## 5) Verification CSV Meaning

Common CSVs include:

- `fr_36_predictions.csv` (or similar naming) 
 Baseline predictions from original FR 36 model.

- `*_tfserving_fr_36_predictions.csv` 
 Predictions from TF Serving model endpoint/export.

- `*complete_fr36_and_tf216_scores.csv` 
 Main consolidated file to compare FR 36 and TF 2.16 scores.

Use these files to confirm conversion quality and detect drift.

---

## 7) Environment Setup

This repo keeps separate requirements for compatibility isolation:

- `fr_36_requirements.txt` → FR 36 validation/conversion context
- `tf_216_requirements.txt` → TensorFlow 2.16 conversion/validation context

Recommended: create separate virtual environments for each requirements file.

---

Whether you're new to the gym or a seasoned pro, you've probably wondered: How many different exercises should I be doing in each workout? The answer, as is often the case with fitness, isn't one-size-fits-all. But don't worry, we're going to break it down and help you find your sweet spot.

Optimal number of exercises per workout

Including the right number of exercises in your workouts can make a big difference.

Too few exercises and you might not challenge yourself enough to see the progress you want to. This can then lead to plateaus and a lack of motivation. You also might not be working all your major muscle groups, which can hinder your overall fitness goals.

Too many exercises, on the other hand, can lead to overdoing it in a major way. This can mean you don't give your muscles enough time to recover from the stress of exercise. Overtraining like this can lead to fatigue, decreased performance, and even injuries. It can also make your workouts feel overwhelming and destroy your motivation to go to the gym.

The key is to find the balance that allows you to progressively overload your muscles (gradually increase the difficulty of your workouts) while still allowing time for a proper recovery. This will help you make consistent progress towards your fitness goals and keep you coming back session after session.

Gym equipment guides

Our Personal Trainers guide your form and keep you Master gym machines with our guides! Learn proper form, avoid mistakes, and boost your results.

Some exercise guidelines

There are a few things you need to think about when deciding how many exercises to include in your workout.

Your fitness level

This is a big one! Beginners should focus on mastering proper form for a smaller number of exercises to avoid injury and build a solid foundation. You can gradually increase the number of exercises as you get stronger and more comfortable with compound movements like squats, lunges, pushes, pulls, and core exercises. These exercises work multiple muscle groups at once, making them a great time-efficient option for everyone.

Your goals

Are you aiming to build muscle, increase strength, improve cardiovascular fitness, or a combination of these? Each goal will benefit from a slightly different approach to exercise type and volume. For example, strength training programs usually focus on compound movements with fewer repetitions at heavier weights, while muscle-building programs will include more isolation exercises and a higher number of reps.

The type of workout

Full-body workouts, which hit all the major muscle groups in one session, are a great option for beginners or those short on time. These workouts typically involve fewer exercises per muscle group compared to split routines (where you train different muscle groups on different days). A Split routine will allow you to target a specific muscle group with greater intensity, but it will also require more time at the gym each week.

Recovery time

Don't forget to factor in rest days, they are just as important as the days you spend hitting the gym. Your muscles need time to repair and rebuild themselves after a workout, this is when all that muscle growth happens! As a general rule, beginners might need more rest days (2-3) than experienced gym-goers (1-2). But everyone is different so listen to your body – if you're feeling sore or fatigued, take an extra day to rest.

How many exercises for beginners and beyond

While there's no magic number, we’ve put some general guidelines together to get you started:

Beginners (the first 1-3 months of hitting the gym)

Focus on mastering proper form for 2-3 compound exercises per muscle group. This might involve exercises like squats, lunges, pushes ( including push-ups or bench press variations), pulls (like rows or pull-ups), and core exercises (planks or crunches). You can also incorporate full-body exercises that will work multiple muscle groups at once, such as burpees or kettlebell swings.

Intermediate (3-6 months of gym trips)

As you get stronger and more comfortable with the compound movements you’ve been practising; you can increase the number of exercises to 3-4 per muscle group. Start adding some isolation exercises so you can target specific muscles in more detail. This could include things like bicep curls, tricep extensions, shoulder raises, or calf raises. Make sure you maintain a balance between compound and isolation exercises, with compound movements making up the bulk of your workout routine.

Advanced (6+ months of regular gym workouts)

By this stage, you can probably handle a higher training volume. So, increase the number of exercises to 4-5 per muscle group, but prioritise quality over quantity. Focus on using challenging weights and maintaining proper form throughout each set and repetition. Some advanced lifters might also experiment with more advanced training techniques, such as drop sets or supersets, to further challenge their muscles.

 To hit your goals—a V-taper, a defined body, and losing the tummy/love handles—we need to focus on two things: widening your shoulders and lats (upper back) to create the "V" shape, and keeping your heart rate up to burn fat. This keeps the intensity high, pushes muscle growth, and gives you a cardiovascular fat-burning effect at the same time. 

 Here is your 5-day split, designed for muscle growth (3-4 sets, 8-12 reps) and packed into your busy schedule. 

 The 45-Minute Daily Blueprint 

 Warm-up (3-4 mins): Quick dynamic movements (arm circles, bodyweight squats, jumping jacks) to get the blood flowing. 

 Lifting (30 mins): 3 to 4 exercises max. Stick strictly to 1-minute rests. 

 Cardio/Core Finisher (5-10 mins): High intensity to burn off the love handles. 

 Day 1: Back & Biceps (The "Wings" Day) 

 The goal here is to build your latissimus dorsi (lats) to make your back physically wider, which instantly makes your waist look smaller. 

 Pull-ups (Compound) | 3 Sets | 8-10 Reps

 Anatomy POV: This is the king of the V-taper. When you pull your body weight up, your lats do the heavy lifting. Growing these muscles gives you those wide "wings" under your arms. 

 Dumbbell Rows (Compound) | 3 Sets | 8-12 Reps

 Anatomy POV: Pull-ups build width, but rows build thickness. This engages the middle of your back (rhomboids and traps) so you don't look flat from a side profile. 

 Bicep Curls (Isolation) | 3 Sets | 10-12 Reps

 Anatomy POV: Since your biceps already helped with the pulling movements above, we isolate them here to finish them off and create that defined arm bump. 

 Finisher: 5 minutes of jump rope or fast paced stair-climbing. 

 Day 2: Chest & Triceps (The Armor Day) 

 Building a full chest pushes your upper body out, contributing to that broad, defined upper-body look. 

 Bench Press (Compound) | 3 Sets | 8-12 Reps

 Anatomy POV: This works the entire pectoral (chest) muscle, the front of your shoulders, and your triceps. It is the ultimate push exercise for adding slabs of muscle to your front. 

 Incline Dumbbell Press (Compound) | 3 Sets | 8-12 Reps

 Anatomy POV: This targets the upper chest. Fleshing out the upper pecs creates a shelf-like look that connects smoothly to your shoulders, enhancing the V-taper. 

 Tricep Extensions (Isolation) | 3 Sets | 10-12 Reps

 Anatomy POV: The triceps actually make up about two-thirds of your upper arm mass. Isolating them here makes your arms look thick and defined even when relaxed. 

 Finisher: 3 sets of 45-second Planks. Planks train your transverse abdominis (deep core), which acts like an internal weight belt to pull your stomach in tight. 

 Day 3: Legs (The Foundation & Fat Burner) 

 Leg day is crucial. Because your leg muscles are the largest in your body, training them burns the most calories and triggers a massive release of natural growth hormones. 

 Squats (Compound) | 4 Sets | 8-10 Reps

 Anatomy POV: Squats force your entire body to work, heavily targeting your quads (front of legs) and glutes. It is a massive calorie burner that helps shed the tummy fat while building a solid base. 

 Leg Curls (Isolation) | 3 Sets | 10-12 Reps

 Anatomy POV: This isolates the hamstrings (back of the leg). It balances out the heavy quad work from squats and keeps your knees safe and stable. 

 Dumbbell Lunges (Compound) | 3 Sets | 10 Reps per leg

 Anatomy POV: This requires balance and core stabilization, working your legs individually to fix any muscle imbalances while keeping your heart rate spiked. 

 Day 4: Shoulders & Abs (The V-Taper Maker) 

 Broad shoulders are the absolute most important factor for a V-taper. 

 Overhead Dumbbell Press (Compound) | 3 Sets | 8-12 Reps

 Anatomy POV: This builds the overall mass of your deltoids (shoulder muscles). Pushing weight over your head requires all three parts of your shoulder to work together. 

 Lateral Raises (Isolation) | 4 Sets | 12-15 Reps (Notice the higher reps here) 

 Anatomy POV: If you want a V-taper, this is your best friend. It explicitly targets the side deltoid. Growing this specific muscle physically widens your frame at the top. 

 Russian Twists (Core) | 3 Sets | 15-20 Reps per side

 Anatomy POV: This targets the obliques (the muscles on the side of your abs). Strengthening these helps tighten up the sides of your waist, right where the love handles sit. 

 Day 5: Deadlifts & High-Intensity (The Shred Day) 

 Finishing the week strong with heavy pulls and a sweat session. 

 Deadlifts (Compound) | 3 Sets | 6-8 Reps (Slightly heavier for strength) 

 Anatomy POV: Deadlifts target your entire posterior chain (everything on the back of your body, from your calves to your upper back). It pulls your posture upright, which immediately makes your chest look bigger and your waist look smaller. 

 Lat Pulldowns or Machine Rows (Compound) | 3 Sets | 10-12 Reps

 Anatomy POV: A second hit to your lats for the week to ensure maximum width growth. 

 Finisher: 10 minutes of HIIT (High-Intensity Interval Training) on a treadmill or bike. (e.g., 30 seconds sprinting, 30 seconds walking).

 Anatomy POV: You cannot "spot reduce" fat from your tummy or love handles with just crunches. Fat loss happens all over the body. HIIT forces your body to burn a massive amount of calories in a short time, pulling from those stubborn fat stores. 

 A quick note on the tummy and love handles: The workouts will build the structure underneath, but reducing the fat on top comes down to being in a slight caloric deficit (eating slightly less energy than you burn).

 When you use from_pretrained , the library needs more than just the model weights (the large .bin or .safetensors files). It also requires configuration files like config.json , tokenizer_config.json , vocab.json , etc., to understand the model's architecture and how to load it. 

 If any of these files are missing from the local path you provide, the library attempts to download them from the Hugging Face Hub as a fallback. Since you've set local_files_only=True , this network call is blocked, leading to the error you're seeing. 

 ## The Solution 

 Ensure your local model directories ( indictrans2-indic-en-1B and indictrans2-en-indic-1B ) contain the complete set of files from the original Hugging Face repository. 

 1. Verify Your Model Folders 

 Check the contents of your models/indictrans2-indic-en-1B directory. It should contain a set of files similar to this: 

 config.json (Model architecture configuration) 

 generation_config.json (Generation parameters) 

 special_tokens_map.json (Tokenizer special tokens) 

 tokenizer_config.json (Tokenizer configuration) 

 tokenizer.json (The main tokenizer file) 

 vocab.json (Vocabulary for the tokenizer) 

 pytorch_model.bin or model.safetensors (The model weights) 

 And potentially other files like .gitattributes , README.md , etc. 

 The most likely issue is that you only have the large model weight file and are missing the smaller JSON configuration files. 

 2. Download the Complete Model Repositories 

 The easiest way to fix this is to download the complete model repositories. You can do this with a simple Python script using the huggingface_hub library.

 from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download

indic_en_repo = "ai4bharat/indictrans2-indic-en-1B"
en_indic_repo = "ai4bharat/indictrans2-en-indic-1B"

 local_dir=f"{local_model_dir}/indictrans2-indic-en-1B",

)

print(f"Downloading {en_indic_repo}...")
snapshot_download(

 local_dir=f"{local_model_dir}/indictrans2-en-indic-1B",
 local_dir_use_symlinks=False
)

print("All models downloaded successfully.")

 After running this script, your models directory will be correctly populated with all the required files, and your main application should be able to load them offline without any issues.

Step 2: Create a Dynamic Tool Generator
Now, create a new Python file, let's call it dynamic_tool_loader.py. This file will contain the logic to read the YAML files and generate the tools.

This generator will:

Take the configuration dictionary as input.

Dynamically create a Python function in memory.

Set the function's name (__name__) and its docstring (__doc__) from the config. This is crucial, as the MCP framework and the underlying model use the docstring to understand what the tool does.

Inside this function, use a generic API client (like the requests library) to make the call based on the config.

Here's what dynamic_tool_loader.py could look like:

import yaml
import requests
import os
from your_mcp_setup import mcp # Assuming 'mcp' is your tool decorator instance

# This is a generic function that makes the actual API call
def _api_caller(endpoint, method, params, headers=None):
 """A helper to make HTTP requests."""
 try:
 if method.upper() == 'GET':
 response = requests.get(endpoint, params=params, headers=headers)
 elif method.upper() == 'POST':
 response = requests.post(endpoint, json=params, headers=headers)
 # Add other methods like PUT, DELETE as needed
 else:
 return {"error": f"Unsupported HTTP method: {method}"}
 
 response.raise_for_status() # Raise an exception for bad status codes (4xx or 5xx)
 return response.json()
 except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
 return {"error": f"API call failed: {e}"}

def create_tool_from_config(config: dict):
 """
 Dynamically creates and decorates a tool function from a config dictionary.
 """
 tool_name = config['name']
 tool_description = config['description']
 api_endpoint = config['api_endpoint']
 http_method = config['http_method']
 
 # This is the function that will be turned into an MCP tool
 def generated_tool_function(**kwargs):
 # Here you could add validation against the 'parameters' in your config
 # For simplicity, we directly pass the kwargs as the JSON payload or query params
 return _api_caller(
 endpoint=api_endpoint,
 method=http_method,
 params=kwargs
 )

 # CRITICAL: Set the name and docstring for MCP to discover
 generated_tool_function.__name__ = tool_name
 generated_tool_function.__doc__ = tool_description
 
 # Apply the MCP decorator and return the decorated tool
 return mcp.tool()(generated_tool_function)

def load_tools_from_directory(directory_path: str = "./tools_config"):
 """
 Scans a directory for .yaml files, creates tools, and returns a list of them.
 """
 registered_tools = []
 print(f"🔎 Scanning for tool configurations in '{directory_path}'...")
 for filename in os.listdir(directory_path):
 if filename.endswith(".yaml") or filename.endswith(".yml"):
 filepath = os.path.join(directory_path, filename)
 with open(filepath, 'r') as f:
 config_data = yaml.safe_load(f)
 if 'tools' in config_data:
 for tool_config in config_data['tools']:
 print(f" -> Creating tool: {tool_config['name']}")
 new_tool = create_tool_from_config(tool_config)
 registered_tools.append(new_tool)
 print("✅ Tool loading complete.")
 return registered_tools

Finally, modify your main.py to use this new loader. Instead of importing each tool manually, you'll just call load_tools_from_directory.

# 2. Register all the loaded tools with the MCP server

No Python: They don't need to touch xyz.py, xyz_tools.py, or main.py.

 The key clue is the file model.safetensors_.gstmp in your directory listings. The .gstmp extension indicates an incomplete download. The library is looking for a complete model weights file, typically named model.safetensors or pytorch_model.bin , but can't find one. 

 How to Fix It 

 You need to ensure you have the complete and correctly named model files. 

 Navigate to your model directories: 

 cd models/indictrans2-en-indic-1B

 Rename the temporary file. If you are confident the download was complete, you can rename it: 

 mv model.safetensors_.gstmp model.safetensors

 Repeat for the other model directory: 

 cd ../indictrans2-indic-en-1B
mv model.safetensors_.gstmp model.safetensors

 If renaming the file doesn't work, it means the download was corrupted or incomplete. In that case, you will need to delete the model folders and re-download them completely. 

 After fixing the filenames, your application should be able to load the models from the local path without trying to connect to the internet.

def _serialize_datetime(obj: Any) -> Any:

async def log_transaction(db: Session, query: QueryRequest, result: str, agent_id: str) -> str:
 """

 if query.session_id:

 # Try to convert existing session_id to UUID

 new_session = Session(

 start_time=current_time,

 )

 except ValueError:

 start_time=current_time,

 )

@app.post("/ask")
async def ask_agent(request: Request):
 db = next(get_db())
 try:
 # Parse the request body manually
 body = await request.json()
 print("Request body:", body)

 # Validate required fields
 if not body.get("query"):
 raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Query is required")
 if not body.get("agent"):
 raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Agent ID is required")
 
 # Get framework with default to langgraph
 framework = body.get("framework", "langgraph")
 
 if body.get("session_id") is None:
 session_id = uuid.uuid4()
 user_id = request.query_params.get("user_id", "web_user")
 session = Session(id=session_id, user_id=user_id, start_time=datetime.now(), status="active")
 db.add(session)
 db.commit()
 body["session_id"] = session_id
 else:
 session_id = body.get("session_id")

 # Create QueryRequest instance with framework
 query = QueryRequest(
 query=body["query"],
 agent=body["agent"],
 session_id=str(session_id) if session_id else None,
 framework=framework # Add this
 )
 
 result = None

 # Validate agent exists if it's a database agent
 if query.agent not in AVAILABLE_AGENTS:
 agent = get_agent_by_id(db, query.agent)
 if not agent:
 raise HTTPException(
 status_code=404,
 detail=f"Agent with ID {query.agent} not found"
 )

 # Create transaction first
 transaction_id = await log_transaction(db, query, None, query.agent)

 try:
 # Check if it's a hardcoded agent
 if query.agent in AVAILABLE_AGENTS:
 # Handle hardcoded agents (unchanged)
 from interactions.agent_communication import AgentCommunicator
 communicator = AgentCommunicator()
 
 if query.agent == "crew":
 result = communicator.execute_crew(query.query)
 elif query.agent == "rag_combined":
 result = communicator.rag_combined_query(query.query)
 else:
 result = communicator.query(query.agent, query.query, query.session_id)
 else:
 # Handle database agents with selected framework
 if query.framework == "crew":
 result = await get_and_run_crew_agent(db, query.agent, query.query, uuid.UUID(transaction_id))
 else: # Default to langgraph
 result = await get_and_run_langgraph_agent(db, query.agent, query.query, uuid.UUID(transaction_id))
 
 
 if result is None:
 raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Agent returned no result")
 
 # Update the transaction with the result
 transaction = db.query(Transaction).filter(Transaction.id == uuid.UUID(transaction_id)).first()
 if transaction:
 transaction.final_output = result
 transaction.status = "completed"
 transaction.end_time = datetime.now()
 db.commit()
 
 return {
 "session_id": query.session_id,
 "transaction_id": transaction_id,
 "result": result
 }
 
 except Exception as e:
 # Update transaction status to failed
 transaction = db.query(Transaction).filter(Transaction.id == uuid.UUID(transaction_id)).first()
 if transaction:
 transaction.status = "failed"
 transaction.end_time = datetime.now()
 transaction.final_output = {"error": str(e)}
 db.commit()
 raise
 
 except ValueError as e:
 raise HTTPException(status_code=422, detail=str(e))
 except HTTPException:
 raise
 except Exception as e:
 print("Error:", str(e))
 raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=str(e))

 <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.0/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.js"></script>
 <script>
 const selectedTools = new Set();
 const selectedToolDetails = new Map(); // Store tool name and description
 let mcpTools = [];
 
 // Add these new functions for edit functionality
 let editSelectedTools = new Set();
 let editSelectedToolDetails = new Map();
 
 // Add these variables at the top with other global variables
 let originalMcpTools = new Set();
 let originalMcpToolDetails = new Map();
 
 let pendingUpdateData = null;
 
 function snakeToPascalCase(str) {
 if (!str) return '';
 return str.split('_').map(word => word.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + word.slice(1)).join('');
 }

 // Function to escape special characters
 function escapeHtml(unsafe) {
 return unsafe
 .replace(/&/g, "&")
 .replace(/</g, "<")
 .replace(/>/g, ">")
 .replace(/"/g, """)
 .replace(/'/g, "'");
 }

 // Function to fetch MCP tools
 async function fetchMCPTools() {
 const statusDiv = document.getElementById('mcpStatus');
 statusDiv.style.display = 'block';
 statusDiv.className = 'mcp-status';
 statusDiv.innerHTML = '<i class="fas fa-spinner fa-spin"></i> Connecting to MCP server...';
 
 try {
 const response = await fetch('/mcp-tools');
 if (response.ok) {
 mcpTools = await response.json();
 updateMCPToolsList();
 statusDiv.className = 'mcp-status success';
 statusDiv.innerHTML = '<i class="fas fa-check"></i> Successfully connected to MCP server';
 } else {
 throw new Error('Failed to connect to MCP server');
 }
 } catch (error) {
 console.error('Error fetching MCP tools:', error);
 statusDiv.className = 'mcp-status error';
 statusDiv.innerHTML = `<i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> MCP server is not available. Please check if the server is running.`;
 }
 }

 // Function to update MCP tools list
 function updateMCPToolsList() {
 const container = document.getElementById('mcpToolsList');
 container.innerHTML = mcpTools.map(tool => {
 const escapedName = escapeHtml(tool.name);
 const escapedDesc = escapeHtml(tool.description || '');
 const safeDesc = JSON.stringify(escapedDesc).slice(1, -1); // Remove quotes from JSON string
 console.log(escapedName, safeDesc);
 return `
 <div class="list-group-item">
 <div class="form-check">
 <input class="form-check-input" type="checkbox" 
 value="${escapedName}" 
 id="tool_${escapedName}" 
 onchange="toggleMCPTool('${escapedName}', '${safeDesc}')"
 ${selectedTools.has(tool.name) ? 'checked' : ''}>
 <label class="form-check-label" for="tool_${escapedName}">
 <strong>${escapedName}</strong>
 <p class="mb-0 text-muted">${escapedDesc}</p>
 </label>
 </div>
 </div>
 `;
 }).join('');
 }

 // Function to update selected tools list display
 function updateSelectedToolsList() {
 const container = document.getElementById('selectedTools');
 if (selectedToolDetails.size === 0) {
 container.innerHTML = '<p class="text-muted">No tools selected</p>';
 return;
 }
 container.innerHTML = Array.from(selectedToolDetails.entries())
 .map(([name, desc]) => `
 <div class="badge bg-primary me-2 mb-2" style="font-size: 0.9em;">
 ${escapeHtml(name)}
 <small class="ms-1">${escapeHtml(desc)}</small>
 </div>
 `).join('');
 }

 // Function to toggle MCP tool selection
 function toggleMCPTool(toolName, toolDescription) {
 try {
 console.log('Toggling tool:', toolName, toolDescription); // Debug log
 const checkbox = document.getElementById(`tool_${toolName}`);
 if (checkbox.checked) {
 selectedTools.add(toolName);
 selectedToolDetails.set(toolName, toolDescription);
 } else {
 selectedTools.delete(toolName);
 selectedToolDetails.delete(toolName);
 }
 console.log('Selected tools:', Array.from(selectedTools)); // Debug log
 console.log('Selected tool details:', Array.from(selectedToolDetails.entries())); // Debug log
 updateSelectedToolsList();
 } catch(err) {
 console.error('Error in toggleMCPTool:', err);
 }
 }

 // MCP Configuration Toggle
 document.getElementById('enableMCP').addEventListener('change', function() {
 const mcpConfig = document.getElementById('mcpConfig');
 mcpConfig.style.display = this.checked ? 'block' : 'none';
 if (this.checked) {
 fetchMCPTools();
 }
 });

 // Form submission
 document.getElementById('agentForm').addEventListener('submit', async function(e) {
 e.preventDefault();
 
 const llmProvider = document.getElementById('llmProvider').value;
 const config = {
 llms: {
 [llmProvider]: {}
 },
 mcp: {
 enabled: document.getElementById('enableMCP').checked,
 server_url: document.getElementById('mcpServerUrl').value,
 tools: Array.from(selectedToolDetails.entries()).map(([name, desc]) => ({
 name: name,
 description: desc
 }))
 },
 };

 // Add provider-specific configuration
 switch(llmProvider) {
 case 'openai':
 config.llms.openai = {
 api_key: document.getElementById('openaiApiKey').value,
 model: document.getElementById('openaiModel').value,
 temperature: parseFloat(document.getElementById('openaiTemperature').value),
 max_tokens: parseInt(document.getElementById('openaiMaxTokens').value)
 };
 break;
 case 'ollama':
 config.llms.ollama = {
 model: document.getElementById('ollamaModel').value
 };
 break;
 case 'local':
 config.llms.local = {
 endpoint: document.getElementById('localEndpoint').value,
 model: document.getElementById('localModel').value
 };
 break;
 case 'deepseek':
 config.llms.deepseek = {
 endpoint: document.getElementById('deepseekEndpoint').value,
 api_key: document.getElementById('deepseekApiKey').value,
 temperature: parseFloat(document.getElementById('deepseekTemperature').value),
 max_tokens: parseInt(document.getElementById('deepseekMaxTokens').value)
 };
 break;
 case 'qwen':
 config.llms.qwen = {
 endpoint: document.getElementById('qwenEndpoint').value,
 api_key: document.getElementById('qwenApiKey').value,
 model: document.getElementById('qwenModel').value,
 temperature: parseFloat(document.getElementById('qwenTemperature').value),
 max_tokens: parseInt(document.getElementById('qwenMaxTokens').value)
 };
 break;
 }
 
 const formData = {
 name: document.getElementById('agentName').value,
 type: document.getElementById('agentType').value,
 description: document.getElementById('agentDescription').value,
 llm_used: llmProvider,
 prompt_template: document.getElementById('promptTemplate').value,
 output_format: document.getElementById('outputFormat').value,
 config: config
 };
 
 try {
 console.log('Submitting form data:', formData); // Debug log
 const response = await fetch('/create-agent', {
 method: 'POST',
 headers: {
 'Content-Type': 'application/json',
 },
 body: JSON.stringify(formData)
 });
 
 const result = await response.json();
 if (response.ok) {
 alert(result.message);
 // Reset form
 this.reset();
 selectedTools.clear();
 selectedToolDetails.clear();
 updateSelectedToolsList();
 document.querySelectorAll('.tool-card').forEach(card => {
 card.classList.remove('selected');
 });
 } else {
 throw new Error(result.message || 'Failed to create agent');
 }
 } catch (error) {
 console.error('Error:', error);
 alert('Error creating agent: ' + error.message);
 }
 });

 // Initialize the form with default provider config
 document.getElementById('openaiConfig').style.display = 'block';

 // Handle LLM provider change
 document.getElementById('llmProvider').addEventListener('change', function() {
 // Hide all provider configs
 document.querySelectorAll('.provider-config').forEach(config => {
 config.style.display = 'none';
 });
 
 // Show selected provider config
 const selectedProvider = this.value;
 document.getElementById(`${selectedProvider}Config`).style.display = 'block';
 });

 // Add these new functions for edit functionality
 async function editAgent(agentId) {
 try {
 const response = await fetch(`/agents/${agentId}`);
 const agent = await response.json();
 
 // Populate form with agent data
 document.getElementById('editAgentId').value = agentId;
 document.getElementById('editAgentName').value = agent.name;
 document.getElementById('editAgentType').value = agent.type;
 document.getElementById('editAgentDescription').value = agent.description;
 document.getElementById('editPromptTemplate').value = agent.prompt_template || '';
 document.getElementById('editOutputFormat').value = agent.output_format || '';
 
 // Set LLM provider and configuration
 const llmProvider = agent.llm_used;
 document.getElementById('editLlmProvider').value = llmProvider;
 
 // Initialize all provider configs as hidden first
 const providerConfigs = document.querySelectorAll('#editAgentModal .provider-config');
 providerConfigs.forEach(config => {
 if (config) {
 config.style.display = 'none';
 }
 });
 
 // Show the selected provider config
 const selectedConfig = document.getElementById(`edit${llmProvider.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + llmProvider.slice(1)}Config`);
 if (selectedConfig) {
 selectedConfig.style.display = 'block';
 }
 
 // Populate LLM-specific configuration
 const config = agent.config;
 if (config.llms && config.llms[llmProvider]) {
 const llmConfig = config.llms[llmProvider];
 const providerPascal = llmProvider.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + llmProvider.slice(1);

 Object.keys(llmConfig).forEach(key => {
 const keyPascal = snakeToPascalCase(key);
 const elementId = `edit${providerPascal}${keyPascal}`;
 const element = document.getElementById(elementId);
 
 if (element) {
 if (element.type === 'password') {
 if (llmConfig[key]) {
 element.placeholder = "******** (existing key)";
 } else {
 element.placeholder = "Enter new key...";
 }
 } else {
 element.value = llmConfig[key];
 }
 } else {
 console.warn(`Element with ID '${elementId}' not found for config key '${key}'.`);
 }
 });
 }
 
 // Handle MCP configuration
 const enableMCP = config.mcp && config.mcp.enabled;
 document.getElementById('editEnableMCP').checked = enableMCP;
 const mcpConfig = document.getElementById('editMcpConfig');
 if (mcpConfig) {
 mcpConfig.style.display = enableMCP ? 'block' : 'none';
 }
 
 if (enableMCP) {
 const mcpServerUrl = document.getElementById('editMcpServerUrl');
 if (mcpServerUrl) {
 mcpServerUrl.value = config.mcp.server_url;
 }
 
 // Store original tools for comparison
 originalMcpTools.clear();
 originalMcpToolDetails.clear();
 editSelectedTools.clear();
 editSelectedToolDetails.clear();
 
 if (config.mcp.tools) {
 config.mcp.tools.forEach(tool => {
 originalMcpTools.add(tool.name);
 originalMcpToolDetails.set(tool.name, tool.description);
 editSelectedTools.add(tool.name);
 const str = tool.description;
 editSelectedToolDetails.set(tool.name, str.slice(0, 20));
 });
 }
 
 // Load and select configured tools
 await fetchMCPToolsForEdit();
 updateEditSelectedToolsList();
 }
 
 // Show the modal
 const modal = new bootstrap.Modal(document.getElementById('editAgentModal'));
 modal.show();
 } catch (error) {
 console.error('Error loading agent:', error);
 alert('Error loading agent configuration');
 }
 }

 // Update the provider change handler
 document.getElementById('editLlmProvider').addEventListener('change', function() {
 const provider = this.value;
 // Hide all provider configs
 const providerConfigs = document.querySelectorAll('#editAgentModal .provider-config');
 providerConfigs.forEach(config => {
 if (config) {
 config.style.display = 'none';
 }
 });
 
 // Show selected provider config
 const selectedConfig = document.getElementById(`edit${provider.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + provider.slice(1)}Config`);
 if (selectedConfig) {
 selectedConfig.style.display = 'block';
 }
 });

 async function fetchMCPToolsForEdit() {
 const statusDiv = document.getElementById('editMcpStatus');
 statusDiv.style.display = 'block';
 statusDiv.className = 'mcp-status';
 statusDiv.innerHTML = '<i class="fas fa-spinner fa-spin"></i> Connecting to MCP server...';
 
 try {
 const response = await fetch('/mcp-tools');
 if (response.ok) {
 const tools = await response.json();
 updateEditMCPToolsList(tools);
 statusDiv.className = 'mcp-status success';
 statusDiv.innerHTML = '<i class="fas fa-check"></i> Successfully connected to MCP server';
 } else {
 throw new Error('Failed to connect to MCP server');
 }
 } catch (error) {
 console.error('Error fetching MCP tools:', error);
 statusDiv.className = 'mcp-status error';
 statusDiv.innerHTML = `<i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> MCP server is not available`;
 }
 }

 function updateEditMCPToolsList(tools) {
 const container = document.getElementById('editMcpToolsList');
 container.innerHTML = tools.map(tool => {
 const isSelected = editSelectedTools.has(tool.name);
 const wasOriginallySelected = originalMcpTools.has(tool.name);
 const statusClass = isSelected ? 
 (wasOriginallySelected ? 'text-success' : 'text-primary') : 
 (wasOriginallySelected ? 'text-danger' : '');
 const editsafeDesc = JSON.stringify(escapeHtml(tool.description || '')).slice(1, -1);
 return `
 <div class="list-group-item">
 <div class="form-check">
 <input class="form-check-input" type="checkbox" 
 value="${escapeHtml(tool.name)}" 
 id="edit_tool_${escapeHtml(tool.name)}" 
 onchange="toggleEditMCPTool('${escapeHtml(tool.name)}', '${editsafeDesc}')"
 ${isSelected ? 'checked' : ''}>
 <label class="form-check-label ${statusClass}" for="edit_tool_${escapeHtml(tool.name)}">
 <strong>${escapeHtml(tool.name)}</strong>
 <p class="mb-0 text-muted">${escapeHtml(tool.description || '')}</p>
 ${wasOriginallySelected ? 
 (isSelected ? '<small class="text-success">(Originally selected)</small>' : 
 '<small class="text-danger">(Removed)</small>') : 
 (isSelected ? '<small class="text-primary">(Newly added)</small>' : '')}
 </label>
 </div>
 </div>
 `;
 }).join('');
 }

 function toggleEditMCPTool(toolName, toolDescription) {
 const checkbox = document.getElementById(`edit_tool_${toolName}`);
 if (checkbox.checked) {
 editSelectedTools.add(toolName);
 editSelectedToolDetails.set(toolName, toolDescription);
 } else {
 editSelectedTools.delete(toolName);
 editSelectedToolDetails.delete(toolName);
 }
 updateEditSelectedToolsList();
 }

 function updateEditSelectedToolsList() {
 const container = document.getElementById('editSelectedTools');
 if (editSelectedToolDetails.size === 0) {
 container.innerHTML = '<p class="text-muted">No tools selected</p>';
 return;
 }
 
 const toolChanges = [];
 editSelectedToolDetails.forEach((desc, name) => {
 const wasOriginallySelected = originalMcpTools.has(name);
 const status = wasOriginallySelected ? 
 (editSelectedTools.has(name) ? 'unchanged' : 'removed') : 
 (editSelectedTools.has(name) ? 'added' : '');
 toolChanges.push({ name, desc, status });
 });
 
 // Also show removed tools
 originalMcpTools.forEach(name => {
 if (!editSelectedTools.has(name)) {
 toolChanges.push({ 
 name, 
 desc: originalMcpToolDetails.get(name), 
 status: 'removed' 
 });
 }
 });
 
 container.innerHTML = toolChanges.map(({ name, desc, status }) => {
 const statusClass = status === 'added' ? 'bg-success' : 
 status === 'removed' ? 'bg-danger' : 
 'bg-primary';
 const statusText = status === 'added' ? '(New)' : 
 status === 'removed' ? '(Removed)' : 
 '(Unchanged)';
 
 return `
 <div class="badge ${statusClass} me-2 mb-2" style="font-size: 0.9em;">
 ${escapeHtml(name)}
 <small class="ms-1">${escapeHtml(desc)}</small>
 <small class="ms-1">${statusText}</small>
 </div>
 `;
 }).join('');
 }

 function generateChangesSummary(currentAgent, formData) {
 const changes = [];
 
 // Basic Information Changes
 if (formData.name !== currentAgent.name) {
 changes.push({
 category: 'Basic Information',
 field: 'Name',
 old: currentAgent.name,
 new: formData.name
 });
 }
 if (formData.type !== currentAgent.type) {
 changes.push({
 category: 'Basic Information',
 field: 'Type',
 old: currentAgent.type,
 new: formData.type
 });
 }
 if (formData.description !== currentAgent.description) {
 changes.push({
 category: 'Basic Information',
 field: 'Description',
 old: currentAgent.description,
 new: formData.description
 });
 }
 
 if (formData.prompt_template !== currentAgent.prompt_template) {
 changes.push({
 category: 'Configuration',
 field: 'Prompt Template',
 old: currentAgent.prompt_template,
 new: formData.prompt_template
 });
 }
 if (formData.output_format !== currentAgent.output_format) {
 changes.push({
 category: 'Configuration',
 field: 'Output Format',
 old: currentAgent.output_format,
 new: formData.output_format
 });
 }

 // LLM Changes
 if (formData.llm_used !== currentAgent.llm_used) {
 changes.push({
 category: 'LLM Configuration',
 field: 'Provider',
 old: currentAgent.llm_used,
 new: formData.llm_used
 });
 }
 
 // LLM Specific Configuration Changes
 const currentLLMConfig = currentAgent.config.llms[currentAgent.llm_used] || {};
 const newLLMConfig = formData.config.llms[formData.llm_used] || {};
 
 Object.keys(newLLMConfig).forEach(key => {
 if (newLLMConfig[key] !== currentLLMConfig[key]) {
 if (key.toLowerCase().includes('api_key')) {
 if (newLLMConfig[key]) { // Only show change if a new key is provided
 changes.push({
 category: 'LLM Configuration',
 field: 'API Key',
 old: '********',
 new: '******** (updated)'
 });
 }
 } else {
 changes.push({
 category: 'LLM Configuration',
 field: `${key.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + key.slice(1)}`,
 old: currentLLMConfig[key],
 new: newLLMConfig[key]
 });
 }
 }
 });
 
 // MCP Changes
 const currentMCP = currentAgent.config.mcp || {};
 const newMCP = formData.config.mcp || {};
 
 if (currentMCP.enabled !== newMCP.enabled) {
 changes.push({
 category: 'MCP Configuration',
 field: 'Enabled',
 old: currentMCP.enabled ? 'Yes' : 'No',
 new: newMCP.enabled ? 'Yes' : 'No'
 });
 }
 
 if (currentMCP.server_url !== newMCP.server_url) {
 changes.push({
 category: 'MCP Configuration',
 field: 'Server URL',
 old: currentMCP.server_url,
 new: newMCP.server_url
 });
 }

 result = None

 # Validate agent exists if it's a database agent
 if query.agent not in AVAILABLE_AGENTS:
 agent = get_agent_by_id(db, query.agent)
 if not agent:
 raise HTTPException(
 status_code=404,
 detail=f"Agent with ID {query.agent} not found"
 )

 # Create transaction first
 transaction_id = await log_transaction(db, query, None, query.agent)

 try:
 # Check if it's a hardcoded agent
 if query.agent in AVAILABLE_AGENTS:
 # Handle hardcoded agents (unchanged)
 from interactions.agent_communication import AgentCommunicator
 communicator = AgentCommunicator()
 
 if query.agent == "crew":
 result = communicator.execute_crew(query.query)
 elif query.agent == "rag_combined":
 result = communicator.rag_combined_query(query.query)
 else:
 result = communicator.query(query.agent, query.query, query.session_id)
 else:
 # Handle database agents with selected framework
 if query.framework == "crew":
 result = await get_and_run_crew_agent(db, query.agent, query.query, uuid.UUID(transaction_id))
 else: # Default to langgraph
 result = await get_and_run_langgraph_agent(db, query.agent, query.query, uuid.UUID(transaction_id))
 
 
 if result is None:
 raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Agent returned no result")
 
 # Update the transaction with the result
 transaction = db.query(Transaction).filter(Transaction.id == uuid.UUID(transaction_id)).first()
 if transaction:
 transaction.final_output = result
 transaction.status = "completed"
 transaction.end_time = datetime.now()
 db.commit()
 
 return {
 "session_id": query.session_id,
 "transaction_id": transaction_id,
 "result": result
 }
 
 except Exception as e:
 # Update transaction status to failed
 transaction = db.query(Transaction).filter(Transaction.id == uuid.UUID(transaction_id)).first()
 if transaction:

 transaction.end_time = datetime.now()
 transaction.final_output = {"error": str(e)}
 db.commit()
 raise
 
 except ValueError as e:
 raise HTTPException(status_code=422, detail=str(e))
 except HTTPException:
 raise
 except Exception as e:

 raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=str(e))
